overview: A Pacific Northwest storm brings snow to Utah through Saturday, shifting north over time. Colorado gets a southwest-flow system Friday night into Saturday, with a second weaker disturbance around Monday into Tuesday.

regions.title: Wasatch
regions.text: A Pacific Northwest storm crosses Utah in pieces through early Saturday, with snow focused on northern Utah as it moves on. Friday is the main day, when snow levels drop and the heaviest bursts arrive. Snowbasin has the biggest total at 10". The NWS is calling for more, 12 to 19 inches Friday through Friday night. A Winter Storm Warning runs Thursday to Saturday.

regions.title: Central Rockies
regions.text: Moisture from the Pacific Northwest storm reaches western Colorado Thursday night and Friday on strong southwest winds. The snow is banded and showery, so amounts vary a lot from one range to the next. Telluride has the biggest total at 8", and the wind is a real factor, with gusts up to 55 mph Friday. Expect blowing snow and poor visibility on exposed ridges.

regions.title: Southern Rockies
regions.text: Strong winds hit the southern Sangres and the I-25 gap areas Friday, with a High Wind Warning for the Sangres. Wolf Creek is the snowiest resort at 7", with blowing snow likely Friday and Friday night. A quick system arrives Friday night with snow showers for the Continental Divide. Taos sees light snow showers Saturday.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Coastal British Columbia runs wetter and milder, with a mix of rain and snow. Cypress Mountain is the biggest total at 7", with its main snow on Sunday. Whistler gets periods of snow through the weekend and into Tuesday, with rain mixing in at times.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
